tutorials.title: Plan, prove and hand off a task with the CLI
tutorials.seoTitle: SpecWeave CLI workflow: increment, claim, done and handoff
tutorials.summary: A real SpecWeave run in a disposable repository: create an increment, claim its task, prove it with tests, hand off, and pick up the next task in a clean clone.
tutorials.outcome: You see the whole loop once: the plan, the claim, the test evidence and the handoff all travel with the repository.

chapters.title: Pick up in a clean clone

steps: Create an increment with `specweave create-increment "title"`, then write the problem, the acceptance criteria and a task with its exact files and test command in spec.md.
Claim the task with `specweave task claim T-01`, so everyone can see who owns it.
Implement the change and run the tests. In the recording, both tests pass.
Commit, then run `specweave task done T-01 --run "<test command>"`. SpecWeave runs the command again and keeps its output as evidence.
Stop with `specweave handoff --reason "<why>"`. The recording keeps everything local instead of pushing.
In another clone, run `specweave pickup`. It prints the next task with its acceptance criteria.
tutorials.note: Actual CLI output from a disposable repository, SpecWeave 3.0.6: two passing tests, one of two tasks complete, and a local handoff into a clean clone. No remote push or production changes. AI narration in the author’s cloned voice; music: “Make Funk” by HoliznaCC0, CC0.

tutorials.title: See how SpecWithCode runs your agents
tutorials.seoTitle: How SpecWithCode works: machines, subscriptions, limits and threads
tutorials.summary: Each of your machines can hold several AI subscriptions, and every session runs on the machine itself. SpecWithCode connects the machines over Tailscale, watches every limit, and lets one coordinator per project start threads that open their own pull requests. Auto-resolve closes a thread only once it is merged, green and approved.
tutorials.outcome: You know how machines, subscriptions, usage limits, the coordinator and its threads fit together before you install.

chapters.title: More AI than you can use
Only one subscription? Pick its host

steps: Sign each machine in with the official tools. Keep every machine signed in to one account per provider for good, for example Claude Code on one account and Codex on another, and add machines when you need more capacity instead of switching subscriptions by hand.
If you have one subscription, run it on the machine with the most free memory and disk, because every session runs on that machine.
Connect your machines privately. Each machine runs its own SpecWithCode server.
Watch the limits: SpecWithCode shows session and weekly usage, banked resets and credits for every account. When one runs out, a thread waits for the reset or moves to another provider or machine.
In a project, talk to one coordinator. It plans, then starts threads for the work, each on the machine and model that fits, and each thread opens its own pull request.
Open a thread to see what it ran and what it is waiting on. A thread resolves itself only when its pull requests are merged, checks pass and the review is approved.
tutorials.note: Recorded on SpecWithCode 1.0.5 with the author's real EasyChamp project, 12 October 2026, through a read-only session; the thread pane is sped up 1.6x and hostnames are masked. Stock footage is from Pexels, the diagrams are animated, the music is AI-generated, and the narration is AI in the author's cloned voice. Since this recording, machines join over Tailscale with an invite line made in the app, and the other connection routes the video mentions are no longer the setup path. The limits chapter (Limits, CLIProxyAPI and fallbacks) also predates the current advice: keep each machine signed in to one account per provider, and add a machine for more capacity instead of switching subscriptions on one.

tutorials.title: Run a project with a coordinator and workers
tutorials.seoTitle: SpecWithCode projects: a Codex coordinator and a Claude worker
tutorials.summary: A Codex coordinator and a Claude worker in one project: model defaults, routing history, resolving and reopening threads, and token usage by model.
tutorials.outcome: You can tell the coordinator and worker models apart, follow the routing history, resolve and reopen a thread, and read token usage by model.
prerequisites: Claude Code and Codex signed in
steps: Set the coordinator and worker defaults separately. Existing threads keep their own model choices.
Talk to the coordinator. Its conversation stays in the project and keeps the routing history.
Open a worker thread on the right to see its details while the coordinator stays in view.
Choose Resolve when work is finished. History is kept, and Reopen brings the same thread back when related work returns.
Open Usage to compare coordinator and worker token totals by model. Cache reporting can be incomplete, and an API-equivalent cost is not money paid.
tutorials.note: Actual application footage with synthetic projects, recorded headlessly on 9 October 2026. Captioned, no sound.

tutorials.title: Plan, verify and schedule project work
tutorials.seoTitle: SpecWithCode plans and routines: verification receipts and scheduling
tutorials.summary: Write a short plan with one acceptance criterion, run a real verification that fails and then passes, and keep routines scoped to their project.
tutorials.outcome: You add a plan with one acceptance criterion, see a failed verification stay failed, record a passing attempt, and keep routines scoped to their project.
steps: Add a plan when acceptance needs evidence: a short spec, one acceptance criterion and a task. Ordinary chat does not need one.
Review the executable and its literal arguments before saving the verification command. Saving does not run it.
Run verification. A nonzero exit stays failed, and that receipt is kept unchanged.
Fix the cause, then choose a new attempt. The new receipt records the successful exit; Recheck reads the same receipt without running it again.
If the repository already has a SpecWeave ledger, it stays authoritative.
Routines keep their project and host. Pause the project to refuse new work; a turn already running is not killed.
Deleting a project needs its exact name and leaves its source folder intact.
tutorials.note: Actual application footage with synthetic projects, recorded headlessly on 9 October 2026. Captioned, no sound.

tutorials.title: Keep project memory and read honest usage
tutorials.seoTitle: SpecWithCode project memory and usage from recorded turns
tutorials.summary: Keep a project's goal, instructions and durable decisions in small memory files, then read usage that comes only from recorded provider turns.
tutorials.outcome: You keep a project goal, instructions and decisions in small memory files and read usage that comes only from recorded provider turns.
steps: Keep the project goal, instructions and durable facts together. Instructions guide future turns; they do not replace a provider’s own history.
Give a lasting decision its own small Markdown file and save it. SpecWithCode checks the file revision before replacing it.
Reload and reopen the file to confirm the decision persisted. Another project keeps its own memory.
Read usage, which comes from recorded provider turns. Missing data stays visible, and a cost estimate is not a bill.
tutorials.note: Actual application footage with synthetic projects, recorded headlessly on 9 October 2026. Captioned, no sound.

tutorials.title: Continue a thread on Codex at a usage limit
tutorials.seoTitle: SpecWithCode tour: coordinator, workers and continuing on Codex
tutorials.summary: A project coordinator splits work between Codex and Claude workers, the results come back to one conversation, and a Claude thread at its usage limit continues on Codex with its context.
tutorials.outcome: You see a coordinator split work between Codex and Claude, and a Claude thread at its limit continue on Codex with its context.

chapters.title: Each job gets the model that fits
Results come back to one conversation
Hit a limit, continue on Codex

steps: Give the coordinator a goal. It starts a worker for each part and lists them with the threads.
Each job gets the model that fits: in the recording, Codex writes tip.py while Claude writes the README.
Results come back to one conversation, where the coordinator checks each worker’s output against the goal.
When Claude runs out, Continue with Codex carries the conversation over.
tutorials.note: Screen recordings on a Mac, 10 October 2026. No sound; the usage limit in the handoff clip is simulated. Recorded before SpecWithCode 1.0.0, so some labels have changed.

tutorials.title: Set up a personal project with folders and tools
tutorials.seoTitle: SpecWithCode personal projects, folders, repositories and MCP tools
tutorials.summary: A Personal project with app-managed storage: add a folder, link a repository, discover a local MCP command and grant exactly the tools it may use.
tutorials.outcome: You create a personal project, add a folder and a repository, and grant a local MCP command exactly the tools it may use.
steps: Start a Personal project. It uses app-managed storage on its device and needs no Git repository.
Add an existing folder and save its access grant. The folder is not moved.
Add a repository URL and associate your local checkout. Match checks the checkout’s actual remote.
Save a local MCP command, then choose Check to discover its tools. Check does not verify an external account.
Grant exactly the tools this project may use. Revoke removes future access; restoring needs a new check and new grants.
tutorials.note: Actual application footage with synthetic projects, recorded headlessly on 9 October 2026. Captioned, no sound.

tutorials.seoTitle: Read an agent result in SpecWithCode: tool output, exit code and diff
tutorials.summary: Ask the agent for the result, inspect the recorded tool call and its exit code, review the file change, and preview the provider-switch warning.
tutorials.outcome: You can find the recorded tool call, its exit code and the file change behind an agent’s answer.

chapters.title: Ask the agent for the result

steps: Ask the agent for the result.
Expand the recorded work to see the actual tool and its output. The recorded command returned exit code 0.
Inspect the recorded file change.
Before switching providers, read the warning: prompt caches and runtime state do not transfer, and the portable chat context does.

tutorials.title: Run your first task with Claude Code
tutorials.seoTitle: SpecWithCode with Claude Code: plan, build and review one task
tutorials.summary: Set up SpecWithCode with Claude Code, run one real task through a project, and review the result.
tutorials.outcome: You end with Claude Code having planned, built and tested one change in your repository, with the ledger line that records who finished it.
steps: In your repository, run `specweave init`. It adds AGENTS.md and the SpecWeave skills.
Open SpecWithCode. In setup, keep this computer and choose Continue. The Claude card should say Ready to code; if it does not, run `claude auth login` in a terminal first.
Add the repository: choose the plus next to Projects, then Local folder, then its path. A new chat opens.
Pick Claude Code in the model picker. The recording sets Full access for the demo only.
Type `$`, pick `sw-increment` and describe the change. The agent writes spec.md with acceptance criteria and a task with its files and test.
Send `sw-do`. The agent claims the task, changes the code and runs the test. The task is marked done only when the test passes.
Choose Open diff to review the code, the test and the ledger line. Then `sw-done` verifies and closes the increment.
tutorials.note: Recorded on SpecWithCode 0.2.6 with a sample project in a disposable demo environment, 11 October 2026; the agent signed in with the author’s own account off camera, and some waits are sped up. AI narration in the author’s cloned voice; captions are burned in. The app has changed since this recording: SpecWithCode now opens projects on the coordinator, with workers in the right panel, so some labels differ.
